cards.scenario: New hire limited to DynamoDB, RDS, CloudWatch now; easily widened later.
cards.ok: Keep user in security group; attach permissions boundary and widen it as duties grow.
cards.bad: SCP limiting the user's permissions.
cards.why: SCPs apply to accounts/OUs, not individual users; a boundary caps one identity.

cards.scenario: Testers deploy a stack repeatedly without broad permissions.
cards.ok: Service Catalog product with a launch constraint role; testers get Service Catalog APIs only.
cards.bad: Service Catalog product with a stack set constraint.
cards.why: Launch constraint sets the role Service Catalog assumes; stack set constraint only configures StackSets deployment.

cards.scenario: Control Tower OUs: ban public IPs on EC2 across all OUs.
cards.ok: SCP (Control Tower preventive guardrail) denying public IP assignment.
cards.bad: AWS Config rule with Lambda removing public IPs.
cards.why: SCPs prevent proactively; Config remediation acts after the violation.

cards.scenario: SAML federation fails after portal login; what to verify (3).
cards.ok: Role trust names SAML provider; portal calls AssumeRoleWithSAML; IdP maps users to roles.
cards.bad: IAM user permission policy allowing sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML (C).
cards.why: Federated users are not IAM users; trust policy, assertion mapping and STS call decide access.

cards.scenario: Third-party customer account gets least-privilege API/CLI access.
cards.ok: IAM role with required permissions, assumed using the external ID in the trust policy.
cards.bad: IAM role assumed by ARN only, without an external ID (C).
cards.why: The external ID blocks the confused-deputy problem; roles give temporary credentials, not keys.

cards.scenario: Dev-account pipeline uploads to Prod S3 bucket allowing only CloudFront OAI.
cards.ok: Prod-account IAM role with S3 write; build pipeline assumes it.
cards.bad: Add bucket-owner-full-control ACL at upload (A).
cards.why: Bucket policy allows no write path; assuming a Prod role grants one and makes Prod the owner.

cards.scenario: Isolated team resources, per-team billing, least-privilege permissions.
cards.ok: Organizations: account per team, SCPs, security account with cross-account access.
cards.bad: Security account as management account with consolidated billing (B).
cards.why: Separate accounts isolate and bill per team; the management account only holds policies.

cards.scenario: Web app reachable only from corporate network, not public internet.
cards.ok: Site-to-Site VPN to VPC + security groups allowing only the VPN/corporate range.
cards.bad: Internet-facing ELB restricted to corporate IP range.
cards.why: ELB with IP filter is still internet-facing; private VPN path keeps the app off the public internet.

cards.scenario: Private subnet NACL for ALB-fronted app; stateless rules.
cards.ok: Inbound 443 from ALB subnet 10.1.0.0/24 + outbound 1024-65535 to 10.1.0.0/24.
cards.bad: Outbound 443 to 10.1.0.0/24.
cards.why: NACLs are stateless; replies go to the ALB's ephemeral port, not 443.

cards.scenario: AD domain controllers as VPC DNS cannot resolve interface endpoint names.
cards.ok: Forward non-authoritative queries from DCs to VPC resolver, or outbound Resolver rule + AmazonProvidedDNS.
cards.bad: VPC resolver as secondary DNS on EC2 instances.
cards.why: Secondary DNS is only failover, not split queries; DCs lack the endpoint record.

cards.scenario: Lambda must reach Neptune (in VPC) and DynamoDB.
cards.ok: Lambda in private subnets in Neptune VPC; NAT gateway or DynamoDB gateway endpoint for DynamoDB.
cards.bad: Lambda outside VPC with a Neptune VPC endpoint, or Neptune security group allowing Lambda IPs.
cards.why: Neptune is VPC-only, so Lambda must join the VPC; DynamoDB then needs NAT or endpoint.

cards.scenario: Central ops-account network; member accounts only create resources in subnets.
cards.ok: Enable RAM sharing in Organizations + share subnets with the OU via RAM.
cards.bad: Share prefix lists (E) or peer same-CIDR VPCs in each account (C).
cards.why: VPC sharing via RAM lets accounts launch into shared subnets without managing the network.

cards.scenario: Private multi-Region WAN connectivity, no public internet, highly available.
cards.ok: Two Direct Connect connections to one Region + Direct Connect gateway for other Regions.
cards.bad: Two DX connections plus inter-Region VPC peering (C).
cards.why: A DX gateway reaches multiple Regions privately; two connections give high availability.

cards.scenario: Most resilient on-prem to VPC link; currently single DX.
cards.ok: Second Direct Connect from a different carrier, attached to the same VGW.
cards.bad: Multiple IPSec VPNs prioritized behind DX via BGP (A).
cards.why: Different carrier removes shared physical path; VPN is internet-based, less consistent than DX.

cards.scenario: Encrypt in transit over existing DX with consistent performance.
cards.ok: IPsec VPN over a DX public virtual interface.
cards.bad: VPN over a private virtual interface (D).
cards.why: VPN over DX keeps DX consistency. Public VIF is the classic way; transit VIF now also works.

cards.scenario: Remote and office developers reach VPC-only OpenSearch from local machines.
cards.ok: Client VPN endpoint associated with a VPC subnet.
cards.bad: Site-to-Site VPN via transit gateway (B).
cards.why: Client VPN suits individual remote users; Site-to-Site VPN connects networks, not individuals.

cards.scenario: EC2 outbound to partner API from one fixed public IP, no app changes.
cards.ok: Private subnet with NAT gateway holding an Elastic IP.
cards.bad: EC2 in public subnet; Elastic IP on the internet gateway (B).
cards.why: All outbound traffic appears from the NAT gateway EIP; no proxy or code change needed.

cards.scenario: Hybrid DNS: on-prem and all VPCs resolve private zone, HIGHEST performance.
cards.ok: Associate private zone to all VPCs; inbound resolver in shared VPC; on-prem forwards to it.
cards.bad: Associate zone to shared VPC only, inbound resolver (D).
cards.why: Direct zone association gives each VPC native resolution; the inbound endpoint serves on-prem.

cards.scenario: Redirect 10 domains by JSON rules, HTTP+HTTPS, LEAST operational effort.
cards.ok: ALB with HTTP+HTTPS listeners + CloudFront with Lambda@Edge redirect + ACM cert with SANs.
cards.bad: Lambda + API Gateway custom domain (C + D) with the E pick.
cards.why: Lambda@Edge redirects per domain/path at edge; one SAN cert covers all domains; API Gateway needs redeploys per change.

cards.scenario: Global audience, optimal read performance, static content, dynamic site.
cards.ok: Aurora global DB + S3 CRR + CloudFront, plus Route 53 latency routing to multi-Region ASGs.
cards.bad: S3 replacing web servers, or Direct Connect between Regions.
cards.why: S3 only hosts static sites; Direct Connect links data centers, not global users.

cards.scenario: Multi-Region app needs fixed IPs for allow lists and nearest-Region routing.
cards.ok: Global Accelerator (standard) with each Region's ALB as endpoint; give out static IPs.
cards.bad: CloudFront distribution per Region; share edge IP ranges.
cards.why: Global Accelerator gives 2 static anycast IPs; CloudFront and Route 53 offer no fixed IPs.

cards.scenario: Only CloudFront may reach the ALB; LEAST operational overhead.
cards.ok: ALB security group allowing the AWS managed prefix list for CloudFront.
cards.bad: Security group listing CloudFront IP ranges manually.
cards.why: AWS keeps the managed prefix list current; manual ranges change and need upkeep.

cards.scenario: Static media with OS-specific content, high EC2 load, slow pages.
cards.ok: Content on S3 behind CloudFront + Lambda@Edge choosing assets by User-Agent.
cards.bad: CloudFront using the User-Agent header with no edge logic (C).
cards.why: CloudFront caches static content and offloads EC2; Lambda@Edge selects assets by OS.

cards.scenario: Refactor batch scripts into serverless microservices, orchestrated, most cost-effective.
cards.ok: Lambda functions orchestrated by Step Functions.
cards.bad: Docker containers on Fargate orchestrated by Step Functions.
cards.why: Steps finish in seconds, fit Lambda; Fargate is serverless but costlier per short task.

cards.scenario: Re-architect video facial analysis with managed services, less operational overhead.
cards.ok: S3 static site + S3 events to SQS + Lambda calling Amazon Rekognition.
cards.bad: S3 events to SQS processed by ECS tasks on Fargate running custom software.
cards.why: Rekognition is managed facial analysis; Lambda is better for ad-hoc tasks than ECS.

cards.scenario: New replicator Lambda must not starve critical functions of regional concurrency.
cards.ok: Set reserved concurrency on the new function + CloudWatch Throttles alarms on critical functions.
cards.bad: Exponential backoff in the new function.
cards.why: Reserved concurrency caps its share of the Regional pool; backoff or longer timeout does not.

cards.scenario: Test CloudFormation changes from GitHub before production deploy.
cards.ok: CodePipeline creates change set, CodeBuild tests, then executes change set to production.
cards.bad: CodePipeline with testing scripts run by CodeDeploy.
cards.why: CodeBuild runs test scripts; CodeDeploy deploys applications.

cards.scenario: Tightly coupled HPC with 800+ instances and EFS is slow.
cards.ok: Single AZ cluster + Elastic Fabric Adapter + FSx for Lustre.
cards.bad: Cluster launched across multiple Availability Zones.
cards.why: Single AZ keeps node latency low; FSx for Lustre gives sub-millisecond file access.

cards.scenario: Least-privilege network and IAM permissions for ECS tasks.
cards.ok: awsvpc mode + per-task security groups + task IAM roles.
cards.bad: Bridge mode (A) or EC2-instance security groups with instance roles (C).
cards.why: awsvpc gives each task its own ENI and security group; task roles scope IAM per task.

cards.scenario: Test new Lambda version with small incremental traffic shifts.
cards.ok: Lambda versions + alias with weighted routing-config via update-alias.
cards.bad: update-function-configuration with routing-config (C).
cards.why: Weighted traffic shifting is an alias feature; function configuration has no routing-config.

cards.scenario: Migrate 100+ small PHP/Java/Ruby/Node apps with LOWEST operational overhead.
cards.ok: Each app on a single-instance Elastic Beanstalk environment, no load balancer.
cards.bad: Refactor to Docker on ECS behind an ALB (C).
cards.why: Beanstalk runs these languages natively and managed; refactoring to containers is more effort.

cards.scenario: ECS CI/CD: fast deploys, minimal downtime, quick rollback.
cards.ok: CodePipeline deploy stage using CodeDeploy blue/green; roll back via CodeDeploy.
cards.bad: In-place deployment, fix by pushing another code update (C).
cards.why: Blue/green keeps the old version running so rollback is a quick traffic switch.

cards.scenario: 30 small Node.js/Python apps, one deployment method, minimum cost, 1-3 GB memory.
cards.ok: Docker on ECS, one task and service per app, service scaling on memory.
cards.bad: Lambda function per application (A).
cards.why: Lambda memory tops out and runs are limited to 15 minutes; peaks last hours. Containers fit.

cards.scenario: Slow RDS reads/writes at peak; CPU, memory, storage free are fine.
cards.ok: Small gp2 volume exhausted its I/O credit balance (baseline 3 IOPS/GiB).
cards.bad: Maximum DB connections reached.
cards.why: Low CPU/memory plus slow I/O points at storage. Note: gp2-specific; new RDS default gp3 has no credits.

cards.scenario: Athena queries on growing S3 data, analyzed by date range.
cards.ok: Parquet/ORC columnar format + Hive-style date partitioning in S3 keys.
cards.bad: Separate bucket per date range (B), with Parquet.
cards.why: Columnar cuts scanned data; date partitions prune scans. Buckets-per-range, random keys, tiny files are not Athena tuning.

cards.scenario: Stateless web tier HA; user stays logged in if instance fails.
cards.ok: ASG + ALB, session state stored in DynamoDB.
cards.bad: Authentication details saved on EBS volumes.
cards.why: EBS is local to the instance and lost on failure; DynamoDB (or ElastiCache) holds shared session state.

cards.scenario: Global serverless app: many data sources, RBAC, low latency, cheap API calls.
cards.ok: CloudFront + S3, AppSync GraphQL API, Cognito groups for RBAC in resolvers.
cards.bad: CloudFront + S3 with API Gateway and Lambda authorizer on Managed AD.
cards.why: AppSync queries multiple data sources in one call; Cognito groups give RBAC.

cards.scenario: Weekly-peak expense app, monthly reports, HA, LEAST operational overhead.
cards.ok: S3 + CloudFront front end with API Gateway + Lambda; data in S3 queried by Athena + QuickSight.
cards.bad: ECS behind ALB with scheduled Service Auto Scaling.
cards.why: ECS on EC2 needs instance management; serverless scales on demand with no servers.

cards.scenario: Lambda to Aurora opens many connections, latency under load.
cards.ok: RDS Proxy on the Aurora reader endpoint + DB connection created outside the Lambda handler.
cards.bad: Application using the Aurora cluster endpoint.
cards.why: Pool connections with RDS Proxy; reuse the connection across invocations by opening it outside the handler.

cards.scenario: Spot HPC DNS updates hit Route 53 API throttling at thousands of instances.
cards.ok: ASG launch/terminate events to SQS standard queue; Lambda batches up to 10 messages for Route 53.
cards.bad: SQS FIFO queue as the event target.
cards.why: Ordering is not needed; standard SQS buffers the burst. Throttling comes from Route 53 API limits.

cards.scenario: Spiky signup writes must not be dropped; keep data model.
cards.ok: SQS queue decouples web tier; Lambda writes queued items to RDS.
cards.bad: Migrate to DynamoDB with auto scaling (C).
cards.why: The queue buffers bursts so submissions are not lost; DynamoDB would change the data model.

cards.scenario: Hour-long file jobs, variable queue depth; MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: SQS queue + EC2 Auto Scaling group scaled on queue length + S3 storage.
cards.bad: SQS with Lambda consumers (A).
cards.why: Lambda times out at 15 minutes, so 1-hour jobs need EC2; S3 is cheaper than EFS.

cards.scenario: IoT sensor writes overload RDS; permanent, growth-ready, cost-efficient.
cards.ok: Kinesis Data Streams + Lambda for ingest, DynamoDB for the database.
cards.bad: Aurora with read replicas, or more RDS storage (A, B).
cards.why: Problem is write latency; replicas help reads only, and bigger storage is temporary.

cards.scenario: Stream factory sensor data, real-time analysis, instant threshold alerts.
cards.ok: Kinesis Data Streams + Lambda analysis + SNS alerts.
cards.bad: Kinesis Data Firehose with EC2 processing (B).
cards.why: Firehose is near-real-time delivery, not per-record processing; Data Streams + Lambda + SNS alerts instantly.

cards.scenario: Weekly ad-hoc SQL over 50 TB+ RDS databases; MOST cost-effective BI.
cards.ok: Glue ETL to S3, Glue Data Catalog, query with Athena.
cards.bad: Copy to Redshift or Aurora and query there (A, C).
cards.why: S3 + Athena is serverless, pay per query; always-on Redshift or Aurora costs more for weekly reports.

cards.scenario: Millions of sub-4 KB records/min, low latency, kept 90 days; cheapest.
cards.ok: DynamoDB with TTL to expire records after 90 days.
cards.bad: Kinesis Data Stream with TTL (D).
cards.why: DynamoDB scales for writes with low latency; TTL deletes free. Kinesis has no TTL feature.

cards.scenario: On-prem Kafka to near-real-time web feed with consistent network.
cards.ok: Direct Connect + EC2 ASG with Kinesis Producer Library + API Gateway WebSocket with Lambda.
cards.bad: Site-to-Site VPN (F) or AppSync with @connections (E).
cards.why: DX gives consistent performance; producers use KPL; WebSocket @connections pushes updates.

cards.scenario: Db2 on-prem, read-only API latency and Db2 CPU licensing costs.
cards.ok: DMS continuous replication to DynamoDB; refactored API on API Gateway with caching.
cards.bad: Rehost Db2 on EC2 with instance-store caching (A).
cards.why: DMS CDC keeps data current; DynamoDB removes licenses and API caching cuts latency.

cards.scenario: Unstructured Oracle data, weekly bursts, scale, reliability, remove licensing costs.
cards.ok: Reserved + Spot Auto Scaling front end; convert Oracle tables to DynamoDB.
cards.bad: Migrate Oracle to RDS Multi-AZ (C).
cards.why: Unstructured data fits DynamoDB's scalable, license-free model; RDS Oracle would still carry a license.

cards.scenario: Move 25 TB MySQL in 2 weeks over 50 Mbps, LEAST downtime.
cards.ok: Snowball native export -> load into Aurora, replicate over VPN, then flip DNS.
cards.bad: DMS full load over the VPN to Aurora.
cards.why: 25 TB over 50 Mbps cannot finish in 2 weeks; ship bulk by Snowball, sync only deltas.

cards.scenario: Move on-prem VMware VM to one EC2 instance, keep software and config.
cards.ok: Export OVF from vSphere, upload to S3, VM Import role, run import via CLI.
cards.bad: DataSync to FSx for Windows, then VM Import/Export.
cards.why: DataSync/FSx moves file data, not the VM image; VM Import/Export converts the VM to an AMI.

cards.scenario: DR: RTO 5 min, RPO 1 hour, cost-efficient, Regions 150+ miles apart.
cards.ok: Warm standby: scaled-down stack in DR Region with MySQL replica and Auto Scaling.
cards.bad: Pilot light with CloudFormation launching web/app tiers at disaster.
cards.why: Warm standby already runs and scales within minutes; pilot light must build the tiers first.

cards.scenario: Move Lambda + Aurora to another account, minimal downtime.
cards.ok: Recreate Lambda from deployment package; share Aurora cluster via RAM and clone it.
cards.bad: Share Lambda functions and Aurora cluster through RAM.
cards.why: Lambda functions cannot be shared via RAM; Aurora clusters can, with cloning.

cards.scenario: Migrate Oracle warehouse and MySQL DBs; cut licensing and operations.
cards.ok: Oracle DW to Redshift via SCT + DMS; MySQL to RDS for MySQL via DMS.
cards.bad: Lift and shift databases to EC2 using Snowball.
cards.why: EC2 keeps ops burden and licensing; managed Redshift/RDS lowers both. No bandwidth issue implies no Snowball.

cards.scenario: Cross-Region DR for S3 and DynamoDB, protect against data corruption.
cards.ok: DynamoDB global table + continuous backups (PITR) + S3 cross-Region replication.
cards.bad: DynamoDB global table + PITR + S3 versioning only.
cards.why: Versioning protects against corruption but does not copy data to another Region.

cards.scenario: 3-tier NoSQL app, cross-Region failover within 1 minute, low impact.
cards.ok: Route 53 failover with 30s TTL + DynamoDB global table + active/passive tiers with zonal RIs.
cards.bad: Active/active tiers on Spot Instances.
cards.why: Spot capacity is not guaranteed; passive tier on reserved/on-demand is reliable. Aurora global is relational with one writer.

cards.scenario: Inventory on-prem servers for sizing: CPU, memory, network I/O, running processes.
cards.ok: Application Discovery Service with agent-based collection on each server.
cards.bad: Application Discovery Service agentless discovery.
cards.why: Agents add network connections and processes; agentless gathers only basic VM data.

cards.scenario: Docs hot 3 months, rare after, retained 7 years; MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: S3 bucket with lifecycle: transition to Glacier at 3 months, expire at 7 years.
cards.bad: S3 lifecycle to Glacier, then a Lambda function to delete old archives.
cards.why: Lifecycle rules can both transition and expire; extra Lambda or cron adds needless components.

cards.scenario: RDS MySQL cross-Region DR, RPO 5 min, RTO 15 min, fully automated.
cards.ok: Cross-Region read replica; EventBridge + Lambda promotes it and updates DNS.
cards.bad: Replicate RDS snapshots and restore from snapshot on failure (A).
cards.why: Replica lag fits the 5-minute RPO; promotion takes minutes. Snapshot restore is too slow.

cards.scenario: Snowball Edge copy of millions of small files is slow.
cards.ok: Run multiple parallel copy commands in separate terminals, separate Snowball client instances.
cards.bad: Copy over USB interface directly (D).
cards.why: Parallel copy operations are a documented speed-up; the USB option is not a supported transfer path.

cards.scenario: Cross-Region MySQL DR with RTO under 5 min, RPO under 1 min.
cards.ok: Aurora Global Database with a secondary in the failover Region.
cards.bad: RDS MySQL cross-Region read replica (A).
cards.why: Aurora Global replicates with typically sub-second lag and fast regional failover; replicas are slower.

cards.scenario: Replace bastions; auditable instance access, no SSH keys or open port 22.
cards.ok: SSM Session Manager: SSM instance role, remove port 22 rules, start-session.
cards.bad: EC2 Instance Connect on fleet, remove port 22 rules.
cards.why: Instance Connect still needs SSH client keys and key sprawl; Session Manager needs no inbound ports.

cards.scenario: Lambda with plaintext RDS credentials in code; secure them.
cards.ok: Store creds in Secrets Manager + Lambda reads them with automatic rotation.
cards.bad: Store DB credentials in KMS and rotate the key.
cards.why: KMS holds encryption keys, not credentials; Secrets Manager rotates RDS creds natively.

cards.scenario: Multi-AZ HA; filter common exploits; send blocked requests to third-party auditor.
cards.ok: Multi-AZ ASG + ALB + WAF with managed rules, logging to Kinesis Data Firehose to the auditor.
cards.bad: Single-AZ ALB + WAF logs to CloudWatch Logs, forwarded by Lambda.
cards.why: Lacks Multi-AZ HA; Firehose delivers WAF logs straight to third-party destinations.

cards.scenario: Remove encryption from an encrypted RDS DB, LEAST overhead.
cards.ok: Export data and import into a new unencrypted DB instance.
cards.bad: Create an unencrypted snapshot, restore from it.
cards.why: Encryption cannot be disabled on an instance, snapshot, or read replica; only export/import works.

cards.scenario: Enable CloudHSM quorum: 2 of 4 officers approve admin changes.
cards.ok: Register signing keys (registerMofnPubKey) + set M value to 2 (setMValue). Legacy mgmt util; CloudHSM CLI now.
cards.bad: IAM policy requiring three crypto officers (D).
cards.why: M of N is configured on the HSM by crypto officers, not IAM.

cards.scenario: Block botnet on Regional API Gateway, known US clients, minimize cost.
cards.ok: WAF IP allow-list on the API + usage plan with request limit + API key.
cards.bad: CloudFront + WAF + API key header (B): WAF cannot limit to 10 requests per day.
cards.why: Allow-listing known IPs blocks the botnet; usage plans throttle per key. No CloudFront needed, so cheaper.

cards.scenario: Most secure RDP/SSH admin access to Windows and Linux EC2, no corporate link.
cards.ok: Systems Manager Session Manager with IAM-restricted access.
cards.bad: Site-to-Site VPN plus SSH/RDP security-group rules from corporate (D).
cards.why: Session Manager needs no inbound ports, bastion or keys, and logs every session.

cards.scenario: IAM user cannot set a public ACL on a confidential S3 object.
cards.ok: Block Public Access BlockPublicAcls is enabled on the bucket.
cards.bad: BlockPublicPolicy being enabled (C).
cards.why: BlockPublicAcls rejects PUT requests granting public ACLs; BlockPublicPolicy only blocks bucket policies.

cards.scenario: Central budgets for team Redshift clusters, alert at threshold, teams see spend.
cards.ok: CFN template with AWS::Budgets::Budget + Service Catalog portfolio per team with Redshift product.
cards.bad: CloudWatch billing metric alert (D) and CloudTrail data events (C).
cards.why: Budgets attach to Service Catalog products and alert subscribers; CloudTrail logs API calls, not billing; you cannot create billing metrics.

cards.scenario: Multi-account EC2 spend spikes vs history, daily alert, minimal effort.
cards.ok: Cost Anomaly Detection: EC2 service monitor, linked accounts, daily notification (verify thresholds).
cards.bad: AWS Budgets with static EC2 thresholds in each account.
cards.why: Anomaly Detection learns historical baselines; Budgets need manually set static thresholds.

cards.scenario: Keep RIs covering 70% of EC2 usage; alert DevOps below target.
cards.ok: AWS Budgets RI coverage budget at 70% with notifications.
cards.bad: Cost Explorer RI utilization report with 70% target.
cards.why: Utilization measures used RIs, coverage measures usage covered; budgets and alerts live in AWS Budgets.

cards.scenario: Logs lost when instances terminate before the 30-minute cron runs.
cards.ok: CloudWatch Logs agent streams logs continuously (batch_count 1).
cards.bad: Shorten the cron job to every 5 minutes (B).
cards.why: Streaming off-instance removes the loss window; a shorter cron only narrows it.

cards.scenario: Cost report per development OU across hundreds of accounts.
cards.ok: One Cost and Usage Report from the management account, visualized in QuickSight.
cards.bad: A CUR in every member account (D).
cards.why: Management-account CUR covers all accounts, so OU totals come from one source.

cards.scenario: ECS on EC2 plus RDS MySQL; MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: Spot fleet with draining for ECS, Reserved Instances for the database.
cards.bad: Spot fleet for ECS with On-Demand database (D).
cards.why: Spot suits stateless containers; the steady-state database gets the lowest cost from Reserved pricing.
